Q4729485.name: All Saints Church, Kingston upon Thames
Q4729485.evidence: The current church was begun in 1120 under the orders of Henry I and has been developed since then.

Q1272948.name: All Saints' Church, Wing
Q1272948.evidence: Its masonry was largely built in the 8th to 11th centuries during the Anglo-Saxon period, making it one of the oldest surviving churches in England.

Q5098912.name: Chilham Castle
Q5098912.evidence: The keep is of Norman origin and dates to 1174, although it may have been built on an older Anglo-Saxon fortification.

Q17526288.name: Church of Saint Helen
Q17526288.evidence: The oldest part of the current building was constructed in about 950 of probably Roman stone, and originally formed the church porch.

Q17529169.name: Church of Saint Mylor, Mylor
Q17529169.evidence: The building dates from the 12th century,  with substantial rebuilding in the 15th century and restoration in 1870.

Q17536721.name: Church of St Andrew
Q17536721.evidence: Its nave was built around 1100, using coursed walls of mixed rubble, puddingstone and Roman bricks, possibly from an undiscovered villa in the area.

Q5116812.name: Church of All Saints, Trull
Q5116812.evidence: The Church of All Saints in Trull, Somerset, England has a tower dating from the 13th century; the rest is 15th-century.

Q5117393.name: Church of St Decuman, Watchet
Q5117393.evidence: The Church of St Decuman in Watchet, Somerset, England has a 13th-century chancel with the rest of the church being from the 15th century.

Q5117429.name: Church of St James the Less
Q5117429.evidence: The church includes some 12th and 13th century work, including the tower, but the current building was mainly built in the 15th century.

Q5117560.name: Church of St Mary and All Saints, Chesterfield
Q5117560.evidence: Building of the church began in 1234 AD, though the present church dates predominantly from the 14th century.

Q5117636.name: Church of St Michael and All Angels, Puriton
Q5117636.evidence: It has an early 13th-century tower, with the remainder of the building dating from the 14th and 15th centuries.

Q5117677.name: Church of St Peter, Catcott
Q5117677.evidence: The Anglican Church of St Peter in Catcott, Somerset, England dates predominantly from the 15th century, but still includes some minor 13th century work, and has been designated as a Grade I listed building.

Q17529229.name: Church of St Peter, Clyffe Pypard
Q17529229.evidence: It dates from the 13th and 15th centuries, and was restored by William Butterfield in 1860 and 1873–1874.

Q17526345.name: Church of St Wilfrid
Q17526345.evidence: The church was built in the Saxon period, probably in the early 11th century, from which era the lower part of the tower survives.

Q17527660.name: Church of St Mary, Stanwell
Q17527660.evidence: It dates to the 12th-century and is a grade I listed building.

Q17530225.name: Church of St Mary
Q17530225.evidence: It has a 12th-century tower, originally free-standing, and included in the church when the latter was extended in the 13th century.

Q5184822.name: Crewe Hall
Q5184822.evidence: Built in 1615–36 for Sir Randolph Crewe, it was one of the county's largest houses in the 17th century, and was said to have "brought London into Cheshire".

Q1252715.name: Doune Castle
Q1252715.evidence: Recent research has shown that Doune Castle was originally built in the 13th century, then probably damaged in the Scottish Wars of Independence, before being rebuilt in its present form in the late 14th century by Robert Stewart, Duke of Albany (c.

Q5313796.name: Dumfries House
Q5313796.evidence: The present house was built in the 1750s for William Dalrymple, 5th Earl of Dumfries, by John and Robert Adam.

Q920068.name: Duns Castle
Q920068.evidence: Duns Castle, Duns, Berwickshire is a historic house in Scotland, the oldest part of which, the massive Norman Keep or Pele Tower, supposedly dates from 1320.

Q5439634.name: Feathers Hotel
Q5439634.evidence: Its imposing half-timbered frontage was constructed in 1619, over an earlier core, for a local lawyer, Rees Jones.

Q5579300.name: Golden Cross
Q5579300.evidence: The 15th-century buildings have original timberwork and there are various examples of early wall paintings and hand-painted wallpaper on the upper floors of the building, still easily accessible and viewable via the pizza restaurant that currently occupies the upper floors of the north range of buildings.

Q764804.name: Kenwood House
Q764804.evidence: The present house, built in the late 17th century, was remodelled in the 18th century for William Murray, 1st Earl of Mansfield by Scottish architect Robert Adam, serving as a residence for the Earls of Mansfield until the 20th century.

Q7069862.name: Nunnykirk Hall
Q7069862.evidence: Nunnykirk Hall is a 19th-century country house and Grade I listed building in the civil parish of Nunnykirk, near the village of Netherwitton in the English county of Northumberland.

Q12064946.name: Orleans House Gallery
Q12064946.evidence: Orleans House was a Palladian villa built by the architect John James in 1710 near the Thames at Twickenham, England, for the politician and diplomat James Johnston.

Q1441598.name: Osterley House
Q1441598.evidence: Originally dating from the 1570s, the estate contains a number of Grade I and II listed buildings, with the park listed as Grade II*.

Q17529438.name: Parish Church of St Mildred
Q17529438.evidence: The church dates from about the 12th century and is Grade I heritage listed.

Q2660524.name: Peel Castle
Q2660524.evidence: The castle was built in the 11th century by Norwegians, under the rule of King Magnus Barefoot.

Q7245490.name: Priory Church of St George, Dunster
Q7245490.evidence: The Priory Church of St George in Dunster, Somerset, England, is predominantly 15th-century with evidence of 12th- and 13th-century work.

Q1990172.name: Sherlock Holmes Museum
Q1990172.evidence: The Georgian town house which the museum occupies as "221B Baker Street" was built in 1815.

Q17743416.name: St Andrew's Church
Q17743416.evidence: It was first constructed in the 9th century by the Anglo-Saxons and retains elements of the original Anglo-Saxon church within a Norman renovation and later Victorian restoration.

Q7592704.name: St Briavels Castle
Q7592704.evidence: St Briavels Castle was originally built between 1075 and 1129 as a royal administrative centre for the Forest of Dean.

Q7593757.name: St John the Baptist church, Kirk Hammerton
Q7593757.evidence: It is notable for its complete, mid tenth century Anglo-Saxon tower, and parts of the 9th century church (the original Anglo-Saxon chancel and nave) which now form the south aisle of the present church, the remainder of which dates from later periods (Norman and beyond).

Q7594298.name: St Mary's Church, Chastleton
Q7594298.evidence: The church was built in about AD 1100 and enlarged in 1320.

Q7594453.name: St Mary's Church, Westham
Q7594453.evidence: The earliest fabric in the church, in the south wall of the nave and in the transept, dates from the late 11th century.

Q17527477.name: St Mary's, High Church
Q17527477.evidence: The oldest surviving parts of the structure belong to the Transitional Early English style of the mid- to late 12th century, but most of the church dates from the 14th century.

Q3603291.name: Waltham Abbey Church
Q3603291.evidence: The present building dates mainly from the early 12th century and is an example of Norman architecture.

Q2409878.name: The Bluecoat
Q2409878.evidence: Built in 1716–17 as a charity school, Bluecoat Chambers in School Lane is the oldest surviving building in central Liverpool, England.

Q7595222.name: St Peter's Church, Bristol
Q7595222.evidence: The foundation of the church can be traced back to 1106 when it was endowed on Tewkesbury Abbey, with a 12th-century lower tower, the rest of the church being built in the 15th century.

Q1683532.name: Jarlshof
Q1683532.evidence: It contains remains dating from 2500 BC up to the 17th century AD.

Q1670559.name: Vinquoy chambered cairn
Q1670559.evidence: The tomb probably dates to the early third millennium BC, and is similar in design to Maeshowe Neolithic tomb found on Mainland Orkney.

Q1641077.name: Kildalton Cross
Q1641077.evidence: It was carved probably in the second half of the 8th century AD, and is closely related to crosses of similar date on Iona.

Q233579.name: Dunadd
Q233579.evidence: Dunadd (Scottish Gaelic Dún Ad, "fort on the [River] Add", Old Irish Dún Att) is a hillfort in Argyll and Bute, Scotland, dating from the Iron Age and early medieval period and is believed to be the capital of the ancient kingdom of Dál Riata.

Q5000477.name: Burrough Hill
Q5000477.evidence: There has been human activity in the area since at least the Mesolithic, and the hillfort was founded in the early Iron Age.

Q6502556.name: Lavenham Priory
Q6502556.evidence: Lavenham Priory is a 13th-century Grade I listed building in Lavenham, Suffolk, England.

Q2920767.name: Lochmaben Castle
Q2920767.evidence: It was built by Edward I in the 14th century replacing an earlier motte and bailey castle, and later rebuilt during the reign of James IV of Scotland.

Q7594011.name: St Leonards-Mayfield School
Q7594011.evidence: The school was founded by Mother Cornelia Connelly, S.H.C.J., in 1872, with the oldest buildings dating from the 14th century.

Q17527676.name: Church of St Lawrence, Little Stanmore
Q17527676.evidence: 1360, but the main body of the building was constructed in the 18th century in Baroque style.

Q1815785.name: Ruthven Barracks
Q1815785.evidence: Ruthven Barracks (), near Ruthven in Badenoch, Scotland, are the best preserved of the four barracks built in 1719 after the 1715 Jacobite rising.

Q4479799.name: Wenlock Priory
Q4479799.evidence: Wenlock Priory, or St Milburga's Priory, is a ruined 12th-century monastery, located in Much Wenlock, Shropshire, at grid reference SJ625001.

Q7809947.name: Tithe Barn
Q7809947.evidence: The Tithe Barn at Cumhill Farm in Pilton, Somerset, England, was built in the 14th century as a tithe barn to hold produce for Glastonbury Abbey.

Q17526847.name: Parish Church of St Mary the Virgin
Q17526847.evidence: The Church of St Mary the Virgin in Pilton is the 13th-century Anglican parish church for the Pilton suburb of Barnstaple in Devon.

Q7594721.name: St Melangell's Church
Q7594721.evidence: The current church was built in the 12th century and the oldest documentation of it dates to the 13th century.

Q5439922.name: Fedderate Castle
Q5439922.evidence: Fedderate Castle is a ruined castle near New Deer in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, dating to around 1474 and built by the Crawford family.

Q950970.name: Dover Castle
Q950970.evidence: It was founded in the 11th century and has been described as the "Key to England" because of its defensive significance throughout history.

Q2363280.name: Abbey of Kells
Q2363280.evidence: It was founded in the early 9th century, and the Book of Kells was kept there during the later medieval and early modern periods before finally leaving the abbey in the 1650s.

Q26827885.name: Aldenham Park
Q26827885.date_text: early 17th century; remodelled in the late 17th century
Q26827885.evidence: That house was replaced in the early 17th century by his descendant Walter Acton. The third baronet married a wealthy heiress and in the late 17th century started to remodel the early 17th century house.

Q2307632.name: Brechin Cathedral
Q2307632.evidence: Brechin Cathedral is a Scottish church building which dates from the 13th century.

Q7594857.name: St Michael and All Angels Church, Mount Dinham, Exeter
Q7594857.evidence: The building in is the early Gothic style and was built to the designs of Major Rohde Hawkins, 1867–68.

Q7595214.name: St Peter's Church, Barton-upon-Humber
Q7595214.evidence: English Heritage date the baptistery to the ninth century and the tower nave to the tenth century.

Q17742126.name: St Mary's Church
Q17742126.evidence: It has a three-story 15th-century steeple with an octagonal spire, but provides no access to the body of the church. The nave is 18th-century and the chancel 19th-century.

Q2294625.name: Greensted Church
Q2294625.evidence: In 1995, however, this date was revised to 1053 +10–55 years (some time between 1063 and 1108).

Q4729499.name: All Saints Church
Q4729499.date_text: second half of the 5th century (oldest section)
Q4729499.evidence: The church was long thought to be Saxon in origin, but recent studies have dated the oldest section to the latter half of the 5th century, making it Romano-British.

Q17525789.name: Church of St James
Q17525789.date_text: c. 1180 (Norman church); rebuilt in the 15th century
Q17525789.evidence: The early perpendicular Cotswold wool church, was built in the 15th century but included elements of the Norman church which had been on the site since 1180.

Q17538091.name: Church of St Mary
Q17538091.evidence: A church was built in Thornton, probably in the 13th century. It was rebuilt during the reign of Henry VI of England, and a tower was added in 1510.
